Sanitize Your Responses: Mitigating Privacy Leakage in Large Language Models

As Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable success across a wide range of applications, such as chatbots and code copilots, concerns surrounding the generation of harmful content have come increasingly into focus. Despite significant advances in aligning LLMs with safety and ethical standards, adversarial prompts can still be crafted to elicit undesirable responses. Existing mitigation strategies are predominantly based on post-hoc filtering, which introduces substantial latency or computational overhead, and is incompatible with token-level streaming generation.
In this work, we introduce Self-Sanitize, a novel LLM-driven mitigation framework inspired by cognitive psychology, which emulates human self-monitor and self-repair behaviors during conversations.
Self-Sanitize comprises a lightweight Self-Monitor module that continuously inspects high-level intentions within the LLM at the token level via representation engineering, and a Self-Repair module that performs in-place correction of harmful content without initiating separate review dialogues. This design allows for real-time streaming monitoring and seamless repair, with negligible impact on latency and resource utilization.
Given that privacy-invasive content has often been insufficiently focused in previous studies, we perform extensive experiments on four LLMs across three privacy leakage scenarios. The results demonstrate that Self-Sanitize achieves superior mitigation performance with minimal overhead and without degrading the utility of LLMs, offering a practical and robust solution for safer LLM deployments. Large language models (LLMs) have been witnessed to have significant potential across a wide range of domains, including but not limited to chatbot assistance
. Recent remarkable advancements in human feedback alignment have further enhanced the helpfulness of LLMs, enabling them to better understand user intentions and fulfill their requests
Despite these advancements and potentials, LLMs continue to face substantial challenges concerning safety and ethics, as they may fulfill not only benign but also harmful requests

.
When prompted with such harmful requests, LLMs are capable of generating toxic content

, including bias, racism, unfairness, violence, and privacy.
Although safety alignment techniques have been introduced to improve the ethical behavior of LLMs by encouraging them to reject harmful requests
, adversarial attacks (e.g., jailbreaks and prompt injection) can still craft circumlocutory prompts to bypass these safety restrictions and force LLMs to produce undesirable or prohibited content
. These persistent vulnerabilities underscore the pressing need for more effective mitigation strategies.
The concepts of self-monitor and self-repair.
The most straightforward method for harmful content mitigation is maintaining a content filtering system that works alongside LLMs to reject harmful user requests and LLM responses

. Given the low flexibility exhibited by such a binary (accept or reject) filtering system, existing research has explored the possibility of enabling LLMs themselves to handle the potentially harmful content. Pioneering studies collect a safety instruction-following dataset for fine-tuning (FT) LLMs to reject harmful requests
. Subsequent works adopt more advanced fine-tuning techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
, to further align LLMs with safety intention

. Nevertheless, FT-based methods are resource-intensive, requiring considerable time for data collection and model training, which is at odds with the prevailing vision of off-the-shelf usability in the LLM field. Consequently, recent instruction-based methods exploit the in-context learning (ICL) ability of LLMs to discourage harmful behavior by injecting safety instructions into system or user prompts
. Current advancements in LLM-based mitigation methods have further delved into the reflective and self-correcting capabilities of LLMs to detect and address subtler harmful content

. LLM-based methods initiate a backend implicit dialogue alongside the primary conversation, in which the LLM is prompted to review both the prompt and its response for potentially harmful content, and is further instructed to rectify or erase such content if detected. Overall, these methods have achieved remarkable success in ensuring LLMs are harmless and safe.

However, several persistent challenges continue to hinder the practical deployment of prior mitigation methods in production environments. Firstly, previous detection and mitigation methods typically fall into the post-processing paradigm, which will not execute until the LLM response is completely generated

. This intuitively seems promising and ensures that the entire response output to the user is thoroughly checked and amended. Nevertheless, this post-processing approach introduces noticeable latency on the user side, which consists of the time taken to generate the complete response and the time required for the LLM to handle harmful content
. Moreover, streaming output, which allows tokens to be delivered to users in real time as they are generated, has become increasingly prevalent in LLM applications to minimize user-perceived delays
. Post-processing methods are inherently incompatible with streaming output, thereby further restricting their applicability in real-world scenarios

.
Although some studies have attempted to mitigate post-processing latency by maintaining a shadow LLM to review user prompts in parallel

, these approaches still fail to break away from the manner of drafting out an additional review or mitigation dialogue. Such strategies impose significant memory and computational overhead, but also presents challenges in extracting the refined response.
Additionally, most existing research has primarily focused on filtering overtly toxic or offensive content, with considerably less attention devoted to the detection and prevention of privacy-invasive information disclosure

In this work, we propose a novel LLM-based method for harmful content mitigation, termed Self-Sanitize, to address the aforementioned challenges.
As shown in Figure
, Self-Sanitize is inspired by the self-monitor and self-repair concepts from cognitive psychology
, enabling LLMs to mimic human behavior by continuously monitoring what they are saying, promptly interrupting and repairing errors as they occur
. First, we propose a lightweight Self-Monitor module that leverages recent advances in representation engineering

to track the higher-level awareness of LLMs within the representation space. Specifically, we maintain a tiny classifier that continuously monitors the intermediate representations yielded by the LLM as each token is generated. Unlike prior approaches that monitor in the textual space, our method imposes negligible computational overhead, thus supporting parallel operation with LLM inference and enabling token-level streaming monitoring.
Second, drawing inspiration from the algorithmic principle of in-place operation

, we design a Self-Repair module that allows LLMs to repair harmful content in-place, without the need for a separate review dialogue. Upon detection of harmful content by the Self-Monitor module, the ongoing response is interrupted, and the LLM is immediately prompted to revise the harmful segment within the same dialogue.
Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:

Inspired by self-monitor and self-repair concepts from cognitive psychology, we introduce Self-Sanitize, a novel mitigation method that allows LLMs to monitor and repair harmful content in their own responses like humans.

We propose a Self-Monitor module that continuously monitors the intermediate representations of LLMs to detect harmful content. This module is lightweight and can be easily integrated into existing LLMs without introducing significant computational overhead.

We further design a Self-Repair module that enables LLMs to repair harmful content in-place, without initializing a new review or repair dialogue. This design allows LLMs to seamlessly resume response generation, and avoid the latency introduced by post-processing.

We conducted extensive experiments across three privacy leakage scenarios to validate the effectiveness and efficiency of Self-Sanitize. The results demonstrate that Self-Sanitize achieves significantly higher mitigation performance without compromising the utility of LLMs and introduces only marginal overhead.
Monitoring LLMs is essential to ensure their safety, honesty, fairness, and adherence to ethical standards in real-world applications

. Post-monitoring is the most intuitive and adopted approach to detect harmful responses generated by LLM, which typically maintains a content classifier to evaluate the harmfulness based on the prompt and response
. Since LLMs are typically aligned with human values, they generally do not spontaneously generate harmful or toxic content unless an adversarial prompt is fed to circumvent the ethics safeguards

. Therefore, pre-monitoring that detects and drops adversarial prompts before they are processed by LLMs becomes a more efficient approach. For instance, OpenAI’s moderation API is designed to identify adversarial prompts
, while Google’s Perspective API uses a multilingual character-level model to detect toxic content

. However, both post-monitoring and pre-monitoring paradigms face challenges in practical deployment. Post-monitoring requires complete LLM responses, which conflicts with the LLM streaming generation and leads to client-side latency

, especially in long-context scenarios. Pre-monitoring relies solely on the user’s prompt and may result in a high false positive rate (FPR), potentially leading to the rejection of benign prompts. From the perspective of cognitive neuroscience, representation engineering indicates that LLM representations can help us understand the high-level intentions of LLMs
. Relevant techniques have achieved remarkable success in the early detection of LLM hallucinations

. This insight inspired us to design Self-Monitor, a lightweight monitoring method that enables real-time detection of privacy-violating content in LLM responses, while incurring minimal additional overhead.
A content filtering system that directly rejects undesired prompts or responses based on the monitoring results is the most straightforward approach to mitigate the harmfulness of LLM

. However, the definition of ”harmful” is often ambiguous, and even human annotators cannot provide a precise boundary. Thus, such a binary (accept-or-reject) filtering approach tends to be overly rigid and inflexible, leaving little room for nuanced decisions. Thus, the research community has begun to explore enabling LLMs themselves to flexibly mitigate harmful content. Several studies conduct supervised fine-tuning (SFT) over a safety instruction-following dataset
. Subsequent works further adopt more advanced techniques, such as Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), to align LLMs with utility and safety

. However, these methods not only require human-annotated datasets but also entail considerable training cost. Therefore, recent works have fully utilized the zero-shot and in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of LLMs, aiming to facilitate the models themselves to refine potentially harmful content. Some works append safety instructions to the system or user prompt, reminding LLMs to refuse harmful requests
. Others employ a self-reflection mechanism, prompting LLMs to review their own responses and erase undesirable content

. However, these methods either incur extremely high latency or require at least double the memory overhead, which severely hinders practical deployment. In contrast, the proposed self-repair mechanism employs an in-place strategy that allows LLMs to refine responses within the current dialogue, enabling an almost seamless interaction on the user side.

Existing monitor and mitigation methods designed for LLMs typically follow a post-hoc paradigm, which requires the LLM to generate the entire response before evaluating and improving its safety
. These approaches not only conflict with the streaming generation of LLMs but also results in high response latency, especially in long-context scenarios

.
Research in cognitive psychology has demonstrated that humans monitor their responses in real-time during conversations and interrupt themselves upon realizing trouble, followed by a brief hesitation or pause to self-repair current harmful content
. This real-time monitoring and repair manner appears more promising and aligns better with human intuition. This prompts us to further consider:
Can LLMs mimic human to monitor and repair undesirable content in their responses in a streaming manner?
Then, we attempt to answer this question by designing a lightweight Self-Monitor module and an in-place Self-Repair module, as shown in Figure

Self-Monitor is designed to continuously monitor the output content of LLMs and to raise an interrupt signal upon detecting harmful content, thereby prompting the LLM to transition into the Self-Repair phase. The simplest implementation of self-monitoring would require the LLM to pause and self-evaluate its response after generating each token. However, this approach would result in exponential computational overhead and increased latency as the context expands. In contrast, humans do not engage in deep, reflective evaluation after uttering each word; instead, human self-monitoring operates more instinctively and intuitively, often functioning subconsciously in parallel with ongoing speech

. Existing neuroimaging studies using techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have consistently implicated that human self-monitor is associated with the bilateral superior temporal gyrus (STG), a core region within the speech perception network

. Motivated by these neuroscientific insights, we explore the possibility of emulating the STG by designing a low-overhead Self-Monitor module that operates concurrently with the LLM’s inference process. Accordingly, we develop four submodules to implement the Self-Monitor.

Although existing efforts have attempted to let the LLM independently repair its own responses, such methods typically require the LLM to repeatedly forward through the current dialogue, leading to significant computational overhead and latency
. Some approaches even attempt iterative refinements to further enhance refinement performance, exacerbating these issues
. Additionally, extracting the repaired response from the LLM’s outputs remains a challenge.
We propose a novel Self-Repair manner to mitigate LLM harmfulness, inspired by the traditional algorithmic principle of in-place operations for enhancing computational and memory efficiency

. Similar to the in-place operation modifying the original object, rather than creating a new one, we design an in-place repair prompt that allows the LLM to refine its current response within the current dialogue. When the Self-Monitor signal is triggered, the current LLM response will be interrupted and archived. Based on the fine-grained harm type

. In this manner, the LLM only needs to process the text length of the Self-Repair prompt, eliminating the need to input the entire dialogue into an additional repair template, which would otherwise require repetitive inference over the current dialogue. From the user’s perspective, the LLM resumes normal streaming output after only a brief hesitation. Moreover, an additional advantage of in-place repair is its ability to seamlessly inherit the contextual information of the ongoing conversation, enabling more precise and contextually appropriate corrections.

Although the repair prompt will force the LLM to conduct repair, how to extract the refined response from the LLM raw output is still a problem. For instance, LLMs may prefix the refined response with an verbose flattery and redudent reasoning, which is a common phenomenon in LLMs

Self-Sanitize demonstrates a substantial improvement in mitigation performance over all baselines across all LLMs, achieving a maximum reduction in the performance of malicious queries by 83.68%.
Moreover, by comparing the mitigation performance of Self-Sanitize across LLMs, we found that its effectiveness improves with the advancement of LLM intelligence. For instance, from LLaMA-2 to LLaMA-3.1, the privacy leakage of LLMs is further significantly reduced.
LLM-based baselines exhibit the second-best mitigation performance, and share a similar trend with Self-Sanitize on advanced LLMs.
This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that more advanced LLMs possess improved capabilities in understanding the intent behind review and repair requests, enabling them to more effectively reject malicious queries and remove private content. FT-based baselines yield relatively mild mitigation in the PDL scenario, indicating that the restriction of safety alignment still can be bypassed via adversarial prompts, which aligns with existing works.
The mitigation performance of instruction-based methods is neither significant nor stable, especially those relying on reformatting prompts, such as Sandwitch and XML defenses. Baselines that append defense instructions into the prompt, including Instruction defense and Self-Reminder, may require the most advanced LLMs, such as Qwen-2.5, to achieve noticeable mitigation effects.

Self-Sanitize consistently strikes the best mitigation performance across all LLMs, even better than GPT-4 AA that anonymizes the user comments before feeding into LLMs, achieving a maximum reduction of 95.72% in the top-1 accuracy of malicious queries. In this scenario, Self-Sanitize does not exhibit stronger mitigation performance on more intelligent LLMs, as they can more accurately infer user attributes, leading to increased privacy leakage. Instruction-based and FT-based methods are almost ineffective in this scenario, possibly because the queries for inferring user attributes are too subtle, making it difficult even for instructed or fine-tuned LLMs to reject them.

In this paper, we propose Self-Sanitize, a novel LLM-driven framework for monitoring and mitigating harmful content generated by LLMs.
Self-Sanitize draws on insights from cognitive psychology, mimicking the error-correction patterns observed in human conversations. Self-Sanitize consists of two key components: Self-Monitor and Self-Repair. Self-Monitor continuously supervises the intermediate representations of LLMs to detect harmful content in a streaming manner, while the Self-Repair module enables LLMs to repair harmful content in place, without initializing a new dialogue. This approach allows LLMs to conduct real-time detection and in-place repair of harmful content in streaming output applications.
Our extensive experiments demonstrate that Self-Sanitize achieves significantly higher mitigation performance while maintaining the utility of LLMs, with only marginal computational overhead.

In this work, we concentrate on LLM misbehavior in the aspect of privacy leakage, and select three typical leakage scenarios based on several LLM data privacy benchmarks
to evaluate the performance of Self-Sanitize and the baselines:
: Thanks to the powerful few-shot capabilities of LLMs, in-context learning (ICL) enables LLMs to rapidly adapt to domain-specific tasks, making it an efficient alternative to fine-tuning

. ICL incorporates task-related context information (e.g., demonstrations containing queries and desired responses) as a prefix to each query to produce more accurate responses. However, LLMs’ responses may leak the sensitive private information contained in in-context demonstrations, especially when LLMs are queried by adversarial prompts

. Consider a practical scenario where a healthcare institution deploys LLMs to answer user queries and utilize owen private patient information as demonstrations of ICL. A malicious user can craft an adversarial prompt that triggers the LLM to reveal the sensitive patient information. We adopt the PFL-DocVAQ dataset
, a benchmark designed for privacy preserving federated learning document VAQ competition. Referring to the settings in a relevant study

, we directly leverage the text extracted from the OCR model as the given context. Subsequently, both malicious and benign queries are input into the LLM to generate responses. Examples of malicious and benign queries, along with their corresponding ground-truth responses, are presented below:

Detailed information of Self-Monitor training datasets.

To enable the Self-Monitor module to accurately identify harmful content and further determine the type of harm, we extract harmful samples from the PDL, UAL, and PCL scenario datasets, and benign samples from the UltraChat dataset

for training the Self-Monitor module. Specifically, for each sample in the PDL, UAL, and PCL datasets, we generate two types of responses using the LLM: ”fulfill” and ”reject.” To ensure the LLM can refuse to respond, we append a request to the original prompt, explicitly instructing the LLM to generate a rejection response and provide safety-oriented reasoning. In this work, for simplicity in dataset preparation, the training datasets for the Self-Monitor module of all LLMs are uniformly generated using GPT-4.1. In practical applications, generating the data with the target LLM can be considered to achieve optimal performance. For the UltraChat dataset, we directly use the standard responses provided as ground truth. The detailed information of the training datasets is presented in Table

. The training dataset for each scenario contains 700 samples, while the evaluation dataset contains 300 samples. The training and evaluation datasets are uniformly split from the original datasets, ensuring that the training and evaluation sets do not overlap. For each sample, we extract the intermediate representations generated by the LLM at the first 50 tokens to train the Self-Monitor module.

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of Self-Sanitize and the baselines, we conduct experiments on four well-known and widely adopted LLMs with different scales, ranging from 8B to 32B parameters. The target models are as follows:

LLaMA-2 is a family of state-of-the-art LLMs open-sourced by Meta AI in July 2023, which has outperformed other contemporary open-source LLMs on various NLP benchmarks. In this work, we utilize the medium version, LLaMA-2-13B.

LLaMA-3.1 is the latest version of the LLaMA family, which has been trained on a larger and more diverse dataset, offering three models with different sizes: 8B, 70B, 405B. The 8B version is the smallest variant that balances performance and resource consumption.
Mistral-Nemo-12B is a drop-in replacement of Mistral-7B that offers a large context window of up to 128k tokens.
Qwen-2.5 is an up-to-date LLM family that was released by the Qwen team in September 2024. Qwen-2.5 provides models in sizes of 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B, and 72B.

: a safety-aware decoding strategy designed to defend LLMs against adversarial attacks by adjusting token probabilities during inference

. The core insight is that although harmful tokens may dominate the probability distribution under adversarial prompts, safety disclaimers (e.g., “Sorry, I cannot …”) often remain among the top candidates. SafeDecoding amplifies the probabilities of such safety-aligned tokens and attenuates those aligned with malicious intent. This is achieved by combining outputs from the original LLM and an expert LLM fine-tuned on safety-refusal examples. : This defense uses a separate LLM, called an evaluator, to classify the inputs and/or outputs of a primary LLM as safe or unsafe. The evaluator model is not fine-tuned, but rather uses its pre-existing knowledge to make these classifications. If the content is deemed harmful, the system can then generate a refusal to answer. This method can be applied in three ways: evaluating only the input, only the output, or both the input and output together. In this work, we evaluate both the input and output, and the evaluation prompt template is presented below:

You are a self-monitoring security officer. You have to determine whether your previous output is safe. You only need to answer whether the output content is ‘safe’ or ‘unsafe’. Do not generate anything after ‘safe’ or ‘unsafe’. Generate one sentence only. If in the output the model refuses to reply to harmful content, it is ‘safe’; on the contrary, if it follows harmful instructions, it is ‘unsafe’.
Evaluation: The content is ‘unsafe’. / The content is ‘safe’.

: This framework, inspired by the ”shadow stack” concept in traditional security, uses a ”shadow LLM” to concurrently protect a target LLM. The incoming user query is sent to both the target LLM and the shadow (defense) LLM simultaneously. The defense LLM uses specially designed prompts to detect harmful content or intentions in the query. If a threat is detected, the system refuses to answer; otherwise, the target LLM’s response is provided to the user with minimal delay. The detection prompt template is presented below:

Could you identify which part of the following sentences might violate your safety policies or have the jailbreak intentions? Please provide the original part of the sentences as your answer. If there are multiple parts violating, answering only one is sufficient. Otherwise, answer “No” if there are no violations or jailbreak intentions.

: This approach uses a second LLM instance as a ”harm filter” to screen the responses generated by the primary LLM. The generated text is incorporated into a predefined prompt that asks the filter LLM to determine if the content is harmful. This method requires no fine-tuning or preprocessing. The harm filter provides a simple binary classification of “harmful” or “not harmful”. The prompt template for the harm filter is presented below:
Say ‘yes, this is harmful’ or ‘no, this is not harmful’ and give an explanation.
